prompt.context: The client, Big Truck Co., is a large, US-based manufacturer of heavy duty trucks, also known as semi-trucks. They make two types of vehicles: semi-trucks designed for pulling trailers, and trucks or chassis used for cement trucks, waste haulers, etc. The company has three marquees (brands), all of which manufacture vehicles for both types. The three brands are the result of acquisitions done in the past five years. The company is profitable, but profit margins have been declining slightly over the last few years. Additionally, the market is forecasting a significant market decline in the next few years, which brings great concern to management.
prompt.question: The CEO has hired McKinsey to help the company better understand their position and to look for solutions for the coming years. How would you structure the problem for the CEO?

clarifying_info.q: How large is the company in terms of revenue?
Can we clarify that the objective is to preserve profitability as the market declines?
Does the company sell into international markets?

exhibits.title: Cost Structure Index by Manufacturer
exhibits.shows: An indexed cost comparison table for a particular product line across Big Truck Co., Competitor A, and Competitor B. Shows index values for In-House Manufacturing costs and Outsourced Parts costs, plus the manufacturing mix (% in-house vs. % outsourced) and total cost per truck for Big Truck Co.
exhibits.data: Big Truck Co. total cost per truck: $40,000; Manufacturing mix: 30% in-house, 70% outsourced; In-House Manufacturing index: Big Truck Co. = 100, Competitor A = 100, Competitor B = 80; Outsourced Parts index: Big Truck Co. = 120, Competitor A = 80, Competitor B = 100

exhibits.title: Used Truck Buyback Program Data
exhibits.shows: Data on Big Truck Co.'s contractual buyback program for used trucks. Shows total trucks in program, the agreed buyback price, and a breakdown of when trucks return (by year) with the expected market value of the trucks at each return date.
exhibits.data: Total trucks in buyback program: 20,000; Contracted buyback price: $25,000 per truck; Year 1: 50% of trucks return, market value $20,000; Year 2: 25% of trucks return, market value $15,000; Year 3: 25% of trucks return, market value $20,000

framework: Revenue: Product mix analysis across two vehicle types — opportunity to upsell or shift mix for higher margins
Revenue: Sales channel model (dealership, wholesale, fleet) — pricing power and margin by channel
Revenue: Three-brand / marquee analysis — risk of cannibalization across acquired brands; potential for rationalization
Revenue: Competitive landscape — where does Big Truck Co. stand vs. peers on price and market share?
Costs: Acquisition synergies — overlap in manufacturing, procurement, and overhead across three brands
Costs: Fixed costs and overhead — evaluate new capital investments that reduce long-run unit costs
Costs: Variable costs — labor (union exposure?), raw material inputs; opportunities for long-term supply contracts
Costs: Lean/operational efficiency — Six Sigma, process redesign across plants
External factors: Regulatory risk (emissions rules) could materially shift cost structure — must be tracked proactively

questions.prompt: Question 2: Using Exhibit 1, what is the potential savings per truck if Big Truck Co. achieves best-in-industry costs for both in-house manufacturing and outsourced parts? (Keep manufacturing mix constant.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should index each cost bucket against the best competitor: In-house savings = (100-80)/100 = 20%; Outsourced savings = (120-80)/120 = 33.3%. Apply each savings to the relevant share of the $40,000 cost base, then sum for a blended savings figure. A great answer also scales to annual savings using volume (5,000 units/year) and contextualizes vs. $30B revenue.

math.setup: Total cost per truck = $40,000; Mix: 30% in-house ($12,000), 70% outsourced ($28,000). Best-in-class: In-house indexed to Competitor B (80 vs. 100); Outsourced indexed to Competitor A (80 vs. 120).
steps: In-house savings rate = (100-80)/100 = 20%; In-house savings = $12,000 x 20% = $2,400
Outsourced savings rate = (120-80)/120 = 33.3%; Outsourced savings = $28,000 x 33.3% = $9,333 (approx. $9,333)
Savings per truck = $40,000 - $30,400 = $9,600 (24% of original cost)
Context: $48M / $30B revenue = ~15 basis points of operating margin (pre-tax)
math.answer: $9,600 per truck savings (24%); $48 million annual savings; ~15 bps of operating margin for the $30B company

questions.prompt: Question 3: What specific actions could Big Truck Co. take to achieve these manufacturing and outsourcing cost reductions?
questions.guidance: A great answer structures ideas into clear buckets (in-house vs. outsourced vs. other) and engages the interviewer by asking whether specific levers have already been tried. Structure and completeness matter more than length.

questions.prompt: Question 4: Using Exhibit 2, what analysis can you do from the buyback data, and what is the potential financial impact for Big Truck Co.?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that the contractual buyback price ($25,000) exceeds the market value of trucks at every return year. Calculate total buyback cost, total market value of trucks returned, and the expected loss. A great answer also probes whether the program may have strategic rationale (customer loyalty, used truck business profitability).

math.setup: 20,000 trucks in program; buyback price = $25,000 each; Year 1: 50% return at $20,000 market value; Year 2: 25% return at $15,000; Year 3: 25% return at $20,000.
steps: Expected market value of trucks returned = (20,000 x 50% x $20,000) + (20,000 x 25% x $15,000) + (20,000 x 25% x $20,000)
math.answer: Expected loss of $125 million on the current buyback program; company is buying trucks back above market value at every return point

questions.prompt: Question 5: What specific steps would you take to address the losses identified in the buyback program?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover both the short term (halt new sales under current contracts, redesign contract terms) and the existing book of contracts (renegotiate, offer service packages as alternatives, sell contracts to third parties). Organizing actions by timeline (short/medium/long term) is highly valued.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions could Big Truck Co. take to reduce its in-house manufacturing and outsourced parts costs?

categories.name: In-House Manufacturing
ideas: Lean/Six Sigma evaluation and continuous improvement programs
Labor cost review — union exposure, wage structure, headcount optimization
Long-term commodity/input contracts to lock in favorable pricing
Facility assessment — age, capacity utilization, flexibility for volume swings; evaluate capital upgrades with long-run payback

categories.name: Supplied/Outsourced Parts
ideas: Renegotiate supplier contracts leveraging scale and multi-year commitments
Audit delivery and distribution costs — logistics inefficiencies may be inflating landed cost
Standardize parts across three marquees to aggregate volume and increase bargaining power

categories.name: Other / Strategic
ideas: Reassess the in-house vs. outsourced mix — shift more to whichever is cheaper at the margin
Vertical integration — acquire key suppliers to capture margin and control quality
Consolidate or rationalize brands to eliminate duplicative manufacturing infrastructure

recommendation: Immediately address the used truck buyback program — halt new sales under current loss-generating contracts and redesign contract terms before relaunching; this can save up to $125 million
In parallel, launch a structured cost reduction program targeting manufacturing and outsourced parts; best-in-class execution could save $48 million annually (~15 bps of margin)
Prioritize the buyback fix first given the scale of loss and the fact that new contracts are likely being signed daily, compounding the problem
risks: Modifying buyback contracts may damage customer relationships and reduce the salesperson's key selling tool — must be handled carefully and with alternative value offers
Achieving best-in-class manufacturing costs will likely require upfront capital investment and organizational change (labor negotiations, new equipment) before savings are realized
An impending market downturn will compress volumes, reducing the absolute dollar value of per-unit savings and increasing fixed cost pressure
next_steps: Immediately brief sales team to pause new buyback commitments and begin redesigning contract structure
Commission a detailed operations review of manufacturing plants and supplier contracts to quantify improvement opportunities
Analyze whether changes to the buyback program affect new truck sales volume — understand the program's true economic contribution before eliminating it entirely
Explore whether the $9,600/truck savings in this product line can be replicated across other product lines to multiply the impact
